title: Stop Anthropomorphizing Intermediate Tokens
hook: Calling the scratchpad 'thinking' imports an assumption. A model's intermediate tokens augment its own prompt — which is why the answer can be right while the 'reasoning' rambles.
key_points: Human step-by-step reasoning leads to a conclusion; a model's intermediate tokens instead extend the context it then conditions on.
That reframing explains a common observation: a verbose or incoherent trace sitting next to a perfectly good answer.
The post cites research challenging the narrative that intermediate tokens constitute a semantically meaningful reasoning process.
Practical consequence: judging a model by how sensible its trace reads is a weak proxy for judging the answer.
Separate concerns worth not conflating: flooding the context window and fighting compaction are engineering problems, not reasoning ones.
content_html: A widely-shared point about reasoning models: the word "thinking" does a lot of unearned work. When a person reasons step by step, the steps lead to the conclusion. When a model emits intermediate tokens, those tokens become part of the context it then conditions on — a functionally different thing. The post argues this explains an experience many people have had, where a model's trace looks verbose or muddled and yet the final answer is good.
extra_html:
Why the distinction matters

If the trace is context rather than inference, then reading it as an explanation of the answer is unreliable, and "the model overthought this" may be describing token count rather than any cognitive event. The post quotes linked research whose findings, it says, consistently challenge the prevailing narrative that intermediate tokens constitute a semantically meaningful reasoning process. It also separates out two things often bundled into the same complaint: flooding the context window and fighting compaction are real engineering problems about budget and truncation, independent of what the tokens mean.

The takeaway isn't that chain-of-thought doesn't work — it demonstrably improves results. It's that why it works is not "the model is thinking," and vocabulary that assumes otherwise will lead you to trust traces more than you should. Follow the linked discussion for the cited papers.

related.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
related.hook: Ask a big model to 'think step by step' and its math and logic scores jump. Reasoning was there all along — you just had to ask it to show its work.

related.title: Chain of Thought Is a Scaling Trap? The Case for Latent Reasoning
related.hook: A visible chain of thought reads like the model's thinking — but it can be an unfaithful, expensive trace. The next wave reasons in hidden state instead of tokens.

related.title: How Much Is Left? LLMs Linearly Encode Their Remaining Output Length
related.hook: Before an LLM writes a single token of its answer, its hidden state already seems to know roughly how long the answer will be — and the estimate jumps when it restarts a draft.

flashcards.prompt: Functionally, what do a model's intermediate 'reasoning' tokens do?
flashcards.back_html: They augment its own prompt — the model conditions on the tokens it just emitted, rather than following a chain of inference toward a conclusion the way a person does.

flashcards.prompt: Under this framing, why can a model produce a strong answer after a rambling trace?

choices.text: The trace is context the model conditions on, not a proof it must follow
The final answer is generated by a separate model that ignores the trace
Verbose traces are always truncated before the answer is produced

flashcards.explanation_html: Because intermediate tokens serve as extra context rather than as reasoning steps that determine the conclusion, trace quality and answer quality can come apart.

flashcards.prompt: What two issues does the post say not to confuse with 'overthinking'?
flashcards.back_html: Flooding the context window and fighting compaction — those are engineering problems about token budget, distinct from any claim about the model's reasoning.
